hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c0.text
The birth of Portugal: Portugal began as a county of the kingdom of León, named after Portucale, today's Porto area. In 1096 it was given to Henry of Burgundy and his wife Teresa.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c1.text
The birth of Portugal: Young Afonso Henriques defeated his mother Teresa's forces at the Battle of São Mamede near Guimarães in 1128, taking control of the county. Guimarães is called "the cradle of Portugal".

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c2.text
The birth of Portugal: At the Treaty of Zamora (1143), Alfonso VII of León recognised Afonso as king. The Pope formally confirmed it in 1179 with the bull Manifestis Probatum.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c3.text
The birth of Portugal: Afonso and his successors took Santarém and Lisbon (1147), then the Alentejo and finally the Algarve (1249). Portugal's borders, set by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, are among Europe's oldest.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c4.text
The birth of Portugal: Dom Dinis (reigned 1279–1325) planted the pine forest of Leiria to protect farmland and supply timber, founded the university, made Portuguese the official language of documents and created the Order of Christ.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c5.text
The birth of Portugal: When King Fernando died without a son, Castile claimed the throne. Many Portuguese backed João, Master of Avis. The crisis became a fight for independence.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c6.text
The birth of Portugal: On 14 August 1385, a smaller Portuguese army under Nuno Álvares Pereira and King João I, with English archers, defeated Castile at Aljubarrota using defensive tactics. Independence was secured.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c7.text
The birth of Portugal: João I built the Monastery of Santa Maria da Vitória at Batalha to give thanks for Aljubarrota. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and a masterpiece of Gothic and Manueline art.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c8.text
The birth of Portugal: The Treaty of Windsor (1386) between Portugal and England is the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world still in force. João I married Philippa of Lancaster, mother of Prince Henry the Navigator.

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c8.viz.events.2.l
The birth of Portugal: João I marries Philippa of Lancaster

hi-portugal.title: hi-portugal.c9.text
The birth of Portugal: The Avis kings launched the overseas expansion: Ceuta (1415), the Atlantic islands, the African coast and finally India. It was the start of Portugal's golden age.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c0.title
The birth of Portugal: Why Portugal turned to the sea

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c0.text
The birth of Portugal: In the 1400s Portugal was small, poor and boxed in by Castile. The rich trade in spices and silk came overland from Asia and was controlled by Venice and Muslim middlemen.\n\nThe Atlantic was the one open door. Prince Henry 'the Navigator' sponsored expeditions down the African coast, step by step, hoping to reach gold, allies and eventually the spices of India by sea.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c1.text
The birth of Portugal: Square sails work beautifully with the wind behind you, but badly against it. The caravel's triangular 'lateen' sails let it sail much closer into the wind, and its shallow hull could explore coasts and rivers.\n\nThat mattered: coming home from West Africa meant fighting the prevailing winds. Explorers learned to swing far out into the Atlantic to catch better ones.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c1.sketch.1
The birth of Portugal: triangular sails: closer to the wind

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c2.text
The birth of Portugal: On open water there are no landmarks. In the northern hemisphere, the height of the Pole Star above the horizon roughly equals your latitude. Sailors measured it with a quadrant or astrolabe.\n\nFurther south the Pole Star disappears, so Portuguese navigators measured the Sun at noon instead and used printed tables to correct for the season.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c2.sketch.2
The birth of Portugal: Lisbon: the Pole Star sits about 39° up

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c3.text
The birth of Portugal: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Ten years later Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India, opening the sea route to the spice trade and making Lisbon one of Europe's richest ports.\n\nIn 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral, heading for India, swung so far west that he reached Brazil. And Fernão de Magalhães (Magellan), a Portuguese sailing for Spain, led the first voyage around the world, completed by Elcano in 1522.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c4.text
The birth of Portugal: In 1494 Portugal and Castile signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a line from pole to pole 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. New lands to the west would go to Castile, to the east to Portugal.\n\nThe tip of South America that bulged east of the line became Brazil, which is a big part of why around 210 million Brazilians speak Portuguese today.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c5.text
The birth of Portugal: Infante D. Henrique (1394–1460) didn't sail far himself, but he organised and funded voyages down the African coast from the Algarve, gathering pilots, mapmakers and shipbuilders.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c6.text
The birth of Portugal: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg were worth fortunes in Europe. The sea route to India let Portugal buy at the source, bypassing Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c6.viz.steps.0
The birth of Portugal: Spices in India and the Moluccas

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c7.text
The birth of Portugal: Portugal built a network of trading posts and forts: Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz and later Macau (1557). Portuguese traders were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c8.text
The birth of Portugal: The voyages also opened the Atlantic slave trade. Over three and a half centuries, Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other nation's, a history now studied and acknowledged.

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c8.viz.items.3
The birth of Portugal: Abolished in Portugal's empire in stages in the 1800s

hi-portugal.title: hi-discovery.c9.text
The birth of Portugal: The voyages connected continents, spread crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes to Europe; sugar, coffee to the Americas), languages and diseases, and began globalisation, with both benefits and great suffering.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.summary
The birth of Portugal: Dictatorship, colonial wars, revolution and Europe.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.q0.q
The birth of Portugal: What signalled the start of the 25 April 1974 revolution on the radio?

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.q1.q
The birth of Portugal: When did Portugal join the European Economic Community?

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c0.text
The birth of Portugal: Salazar's regime rested on "God, Fatherland, Family". It censored the press, banned parties and strikes, used the political police PIDE, and kept Portugal poor and largely rural, with high emigration.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c1.text
The birth of Portugal: From the 1950s to the 1970s, well over a million Portuguese emigrated, many illegally ("a salto") to France, Germany and Luxembourg, escaping poverty and military service.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c2.text
The birth of Portugal: From 1961 Portugal fought independence movements in Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique. Over 13 years, about 800,000 Portuguese men served; around 9,000 died, along with many more Africans.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c3.text
The birth of Portugal: In the 1958 presidential election, General Humberto Delgado challenged the regime. Asked what he'd do with Salazar, he said: "Obviamente, demito-o!" He lost a fraudulent vote and was murdered by the PIDE in 1965.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c3.viz.events.2.l
The birth of Portugal: murdered by the PIDE in Spain

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c4.text
The birth of Portugal: Salazar was incapacitated in 1968 after a fall and replaced by Marcelo Caetano, who promised reforms but kept the colonial wars and the regime's core.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c5.text
The birth of Portugal: On 25 April 1974, young officers of the Armed Forces Movement (MFA) overthrew the regime almost without bloodshed. Crowds filled the streets and put carnations in soldiers' rifles: the Carnation Revolution.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c5.viz.events.0.l
The birth of Portugal: Grândola, Vila Morena on the radio signals go

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c5.viz.events.2.l
The birth of Portugal: Caetano surrenders at Largo do Carmo

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c6.text
The birth of Portugal: After the revolution, Portugal recognised the independence of Guinea-Bissau (1974), Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Angola (1975). Around half a million "retornados" came to Portugal.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c6.viz.events.1.l
The birth of Portugal: Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Angola

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c7.text
The birth of Portugal: After a turbulent period (PREC), the 1976 constitution established a democratic republic. Free elections, a free press and local democracy took root.

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c8.text
The birth of Portugal: Portugal joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1986 together with Spain. EU funds helped build roads, schools and hospitals; Portugal adopted the euro in 1999 (coins and notes in 2002).

hi-portugal.title: hi-pt20.c9.text
The birth of Portugal: Expo '98 in Lisbon transformed the eastern waterfront and showcased a modern country. Since then Portugal has faced crises (2011 bailout) and become a major tourism and tech destination.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.q0.q
The birth of Portugal: How many strings does the Portuguese guitar have?

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.q1.q
The birth of Portugal: Which city celebrates São João with plastic hammers?

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c0.text
The birth of Portugal: The Portuguese guitar has 12 strings in six pairs and a pear-shaped body, giving fado its shimmering sound. Carlos Paredes made it famous as a solo instrument.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c1.text
The birth of Portugal: Coimbra fado is sung by men, traditionally students in black capes, often as serenades. It's more lyrical and academic than Lisbon fado.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c2.text
The birth of Portugal: Lisbon's National Azulejo Museum, in the Madre de Deus convent, shows five centuries of tiles, including a 23-metre panorama of Lisbon before the 1755 earthquake.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c3.text
The birth of Portugal: Portugal's black and white stone pavements are laid by hand by calceteiros. The waves of Rossio square inspired Copacabana's promenade in Rio.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c4.text
The birth of Portugal: Portuguese filigree, especially from Gondomar and Póvoa de Lanhoso, twists fine gold and silver threads into delicate jewellery, like the heart of Viana.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c5.text
The birth of Portugal: In June, cities celebrate saints: Santo António in Lisbon with grilled sardines and basil pots, São João in Porto with plastic hammers and leeks.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c6.text
The birth of Portugal: The Barcelos rooster legend tells of a pilgrim wrongly accused of theft; a roasted rooster crowed to prove his innocence. It became a national symbol.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c7.text
The birth of Portugal: Fernando Pessoa, Eça de Queirós, Sophia de Mello Breyner and José Saramago are pillars of Portuguese literature.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c8.text
The birth of Portugal: Alentejo's polyphonic choral singing, without instruments, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014. Groups of men or women sing slow, deep songs about the land.

hi-portugal.title: ar-portugal.c9.text
The birth of Portugal: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people across four continents, the most spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere.
